stories.title: Cancer patients losing average of €16,200 annual income
stories.summary: People affected by cancer lose an average of €16,200 in annual income as a result of their diagnosis, the Irish Cancer Society has said. It said that people affected by cancer face additional costs and financial burdens, as well as a significant loss of income. The Real Cost of Cancer data was collected from surveys and interviews of people affected by cancer, conducted by Ireland Thinks, funded by the ICS. If found that cancer patients face costs of up to €400 a month on medical expenses, including GP visits and prescription costs. They also face monthly travel associated costs of up to €300 a month, which include car parking fees, fuel costs and toll charges. The ICS said cancer patients reported struggling to heat their homes, fell behind on their mortgage or rent, or needed to borrow to cope with the financial impact of a cancer diagnosis.

stories.title: Further fuel protests not ruled out, says hauliers group
stories.summary: Further fuel protests cannot be discounted as hauliers are unable to sustain current diesel prices, the president of the Irish Road Haulage Association (IRHA) has said. Ger Hyland was speaking after meeting Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris in Dublin this morning, where the pair discussed potential fuel supports in next month's Budget. However, Mr Harris also told him that the Budget is yet to be written, and the continuation of fuel supports is still up for final decision. The cuts were introduced in April following nationwide fuel protests after the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East sent fuel prices soaring. Mr Hyland said hauliers would also need direct supports beyond the continuation of excise cuts, saying many businesses were unviable once diesel went beyond €1.90. The price in many forecourts is now moving beyond €2.10 and in some instances is heading towards €2.20.

stories.title: Rent tax credit to be increased in Budget, says Taoiseach
stories.summary: The renters' tax credit will be increased in the Budget, Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said, while fuel excise is also being examined. The scale of the increase will be closely watched as ministers seek to finalise negotiations before Budget day on 6 October, with Government also examining measures on energy and fuel. Tánaiste Simon Harris said it "may not be prudent" to proceed with the unwinding of excise cuts to petrol and diesel in November if prices remain elevated. The renters' tax credit was introduced in 2022 and has since been extended and increased up to a yearly maximum of €1,000 for an individual or €2,000 for a couple who are jointly assessed for tax. It was reported in the Irish Examiner that Minister for Housing James Browne is seeking to increase the credit by €300. Asked if he supported an increase of that scale, Mr Martin said the credit has been "positive", adding: "We will be increasing it in the forthcoming Budget."

stories.title: H1 profits at Dublin and Cork airports operator dip 6%
stories.summary: The operator of Dublin and Cork airports said a total of 19.6 million passengers travelled through the two airports during the first half of the year. This marked an increase of 1 million passengers or 5% on the same time last year, daa said. But despite the increase in passenger numbers, daa's group profit after tax reduced by 6% to €72.9m as the conflict in the Middle East impacted its retail and consulting businesses in the six month period. Its group turnover for the six months to the end of June increased by 5% to €561.9m, while group EBITDA increased by 16% to €187.3m. The company said that today's results show that its international businesses continued to perform strongly in the first half of 2026 with daa International increasing revenue by 13% on the back of a strong performance in Saudi Arabia, while it also secured a new contract in Vietnam. Meanwhile, ARI secured the travel retail contract at Terminal 4 at New York JFK Airport, which the company said marked a significant commercial win that expands its presence in the North American market.

stories.title: AI, peace and multilateralism on UNGA delegates' minds
stories.summary: The United Nations General Assembly is under way in New York, giving delegates a chance to bring the issues most important to them to the world stage. Luìsa Franco Machado is a digital rights activist from Brazil who founded Equi Labs, a platform aiming to develop a a future "where data and AI serve people and the planet, putting equity, fairness, and accountability first". She is at UNGA to urge world leaders to "listen to our voices". Enene Ejembi from Nigeria is the executive director of Verbatim, a consultancy firm working with development organisations. "The issue the world is grappling with now is around not ending the multilateralism that has underpinned the prosperity and the peace of all nations," she said. Ishani Neotia is from the US and wants greater regulation for AI companies.

stories.title: Kosovo v Republic of Ireland: All you need to know
stories.summary: Kosovo v Republic of Ireland, Thursday, Fadil Vokrri Stadium, 7.45pm Conditions in Pristina are set to be perfect for the game. Little to no wind, temperatures about 15C and no rain expected. It's set to get a bit cloudier as the game progresses, but it's looking like a lovely night in store in Kosovo. With the build-up to Ireland's game with Israel starting, in reality, all the way back in February when they were paired together in the draw in Brussels, this fixture was always going to be playing second fiddle in any narrative during the first half of this international window. Still, there are as many points on offer on Thursday as there are at the weekend, so strip it back purely to football, and this is a massively important game for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side as they try and start their Nations League campaign with a bang. While the match may be playing second fiddle for the Irish public given the fall-out from their game with Israel, it's set to be a huge occasion for Kosovo. The hosts are playing their first-ever game at League B level following their comprehensive play-off win over Hallgrimsson's old side, Iceland in March last year to earn promotion.

stories.title: GAA to meet AFL over player recruitment protocols
stories.summary: GAA President Jarlath Burns has said that a meeting will be held with representatives of the Australian Football League (AFL) shortly to try and find a more agreeable protocol to GAA player recruitment by that association. Unease has been expressed in a number of counties regarding the recruitment of young players by AFL clubs without the knowledge of their GAA club or county boards members. Some management teams have told of only finding out about AFL trials of their members on social media. Kerry county board chairman Patrick O'Sullivan said that the current situation cannot be allowed to continue and called for more regulation. "The GAA cannot continue to pretend there is nothing wrong here. Action has to be taken," he said. "There is a lack of regulation and we need the AFL to acknowledge the work that has been invested in these young players through compensation or equipment or otherwise. We need regulation of this practice and I'm calling on the GAA to deal with this as a matter of urgency."

stories.title: Kelly: Left-sided options a boost for Irish defence
stories.summary: The inclusion of uncapped defenders Liam Kitching and Joel Bagan offers Heimir Hallgrimsson more left-sided options, according to former Republic of Ireland international Stephen Kelly. The squad for Nations League matches against Kosovo, Israel and Austria included three players yet to make their respective international debuts. While Owen Elding is familiar to many from his League of Ireland days with Sligo Rovers and more recently with Hibernian in Scotland, Kitching and Bagan are more of an unknown quantity. Kitching caught the eye at Barnsley before securing a €5.25m move to Coventry City. He was a key fixture in Frank Lampard's side that achieved promotion to the Premier League last term, but the Sky Blues recruited heavily in defence and the 26-year-old found himself out of the first team. A season-long loan to Sheffield United has brought back regular football. Bagan was called into the squad for May's friendly against Grenada before pulling out with an injury.

stories.title: Lancaster eyes on Connacht extension rather than Leinster
stories.summary: Stuart Lancaster said he is in talks with Connacht about extending his contract and that there has been no contact with Leinster about taking over there when Leo Cullen departs at the end of the season. Lancaster spent seven seasons as senior coach under Cullen at Leinster and was immediately identified in many quarters as a possible successor when Cullen announced his intention in June to leave at the end of this campaign. But Lancaster, who signed a two-year deal when he arrived in Connacht last summer, said there has been no contact with Leinster and that he, in fact, is in talks with Connacht CEO Willie Ruane and IRFU performance director David Humphreys. "Honestly, I've not had any conversation with anyone from Leinster," said Lancaster as he prepares for Friday night's URC opener against the Stormers in Galway. "Either them ringing me or me ringing them. So, no, there's no communication there." Lancaster and his wife Nina have settled well in Galway and on the field he made a huge impact in his first season, with Connacht winning seven of their last eight URC games to secure a knockout place in the league and a spot in this season’s Champions Cup when they will face four previous winners in Toulouse, Saracens, Exeter and Ronan O’Gara’s La Rochelle.

stories.title: 5 must-see shows at this year's Dublin Theatre Festival
stories.summary: We asked Dublin Theatre Festival Artistic Director Róise Goan to pick her 5 must-sees from the 2026 edition of DTF, which runs from 24 September to 11 October. We have to start with our opening show, Radio Bette. The Goat Exchange are the hottest theatre company in New York right now, named as New York Times Critics Picks twice in the last 9 months. This production brings together amazing stars of TV and Broadway like Michael Cerveris and Roberta Colindrez to revisit the career of Bette Davis and in particular the iconic classic All About Eve. Expect backstage drama, extreme glamour, Hollywood nostalgia with a contemporary New York edge. Even if you don't know and love All About Eve, If you liked GATZ at Dublin Theatre Festival many moons ago, or if you enjoyed Blue Moon or Sentimental Value at the cinema in the last year, you will love this. Brokentalkers are a brilliant theatre company, who shine a light on some of the most urgent questions of our time, with empathy and humour. In Heroes Of Tomorrow, they tackle the moral responsibility of artists in the a world where truth itself is contested. If you’ve been following the Ed Sheeran/Macklemore/Pink debacle, or if you’ve read Careless People and are keen to think about big moral conundrums, while also being entertained with a witty and thoughtful script, this one is for you. Dead Centre, the brilliant Irish theatre company behind Deaf Republic, Good Sex, and many other Dublin Theatre Festival hits, return with this brilliant show about a man whose nationality changed 5 times throughout his life because of shifting borders and the pressure on natural resources. You will definitely learn something new about European history you didn’t know, but as ever with Dead Centre, the narrative will twist and turn in exciting ways and you’ll have a great time while it’s happening. The kind of show that you want a talk about over a pint/dinner immediately! Last year we had the great fortune to welcome Rebecca Chaillon to the festival with her excellent show Whitewashing, which wowed audiences. She returns with an even bigger show, exploring the search for hope at a challenging time for the planet, with great humour, audacity and BUTTER. It’s big, it’s messy, it’s often hilarious. It’s utterly original and gives an excellent portrait of life right now from a young, queer, fat, black and working class French perspective. If you’ve a habit of doomscrolling way past your bedtime, and you need a fresh take, this is well worth your time. Xnthony makes his festival debut with this cracker of a new musical. Looking at a crisis in faith across generations, he pays homage to those in need of faith and looking for a cure, while perfectly capturing the kitsch magic of a pilgrimage to Lourdes. This new musical has major ambitions for world domination and I encourage you to be among the first audiences to see it. A guaranteed good night out that will make you laugh, and maybe make you cry a bit too.

stories.title: Galway spot named in Lonely Planet's Best in Travel 2027 list
stories.summary: An Irish destination has been included in Lonely Travel's Best in Travel 2027 list. The publication – long the go-to resource for ambitious and adventurous travellers – has built a global following for its recommendations and insider travel tips. Its Best in Travel list is a collection of 50 inspirational destinations and unforgettable travel experiences selected by its global community of travel experts, divided into 25 Best Places and 25 Best Experiences. The editors write that this year's list "reflects travellers' growing desire to slow down, escape the crowds and seek out more meaningful experiences". Among those meaningful experiences is a visit to Killary Fjord in Co Galway, one of Ireland's very few glacial fjords and a majestic part of our national landscape. Located in Connemara, the fjord creates a natural border between Galway and Mayo and spans 16km. It is surrounded by striking natural scenery, including Mweelrea, Connacht's highest mountain which rises up to 814 metres, the Maumturk Mountains and marvellous Twelve Bens.

stories.title: Child trafficking under-identified in Ireland - IHREC
stories.summary: Child trafficking remains significantly under-identified in Ireland, with the number of children formally identified as victims remaining extremely low, the Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission (IHREC) has warned. The commission said the biggest challenge facing Ireland is not the number of children identified as victims, but the number of children who are being missed. Despite growing evidence of exploitation, just 10 child victims were formally identified in 2024 and 18 in 2025. Publishing its new report, titled Child Trafficking and ICT-Facilitated Child Trafficking in Ireland, the IHREC said these figures cannot be taken as an indication of the "true scale" of child trafficking in Ireland. The research found a strong consensus among stakeholders that child trafficking is significantly under-identified, including Irish children, who may be particularly vulnerable to under-identification. "There are categories of children living in Ireland today that are clearly at risk of being victims of trafficking, but they're invisible to the system.

stories.title: Collapse in legal aid certs deeply worrying - Law Society
stories.summary: The number of legal aid certificates granted in July this year fell by 93% compared to last year, according to the Law Society, which appeared before the Oireachtas Committee on Justice today. A new Criminal Legal Aid Scheme was introduced in July this year by Minister for Justice Jim O'Callaghan, which replaced a per-appearance fee with a €520 flat rate, prompting hundreds of solicitors to withdraw their services. In its opening statement to the committee, the Law Society said the new scheme is having a real and negative impact on how the legal aid system operates. It said the number of legal aid certificates granted collapsed to just 702, compared to July 2025 when 10,277 such certificates were issued. Law Society President Rosemarie Loftus told the committee that a fall of this scale is deeply worrying and has been reflected in courts across the country. She said the effectiveness of the constitutional right to legal representation is threatened by the current situation, as the State is required to provide legal representation to those who cannot afford it.

stories.title: School meal scheme to see cold options, new portion sizes
stories.summary: Minister for Social Protection Dara Calleary has said a number of changes are on the way to the free hot school meal programme, including the possible introduction of cold lunches. Speaking at a press conference, he said that overall the scheme is "very successful" but said there would now be a shift at improving the nutritional value of what is on offer. The Cabinet discussed proposals to overhaul the free hot school meals programme after two Government-commissioned reviews revealed shortcomings in the service. Mr Calleary sought Cabinet approval for a number of changes to the scheme, after it was discovered that roughly a fifth of all hot school meals - or around 100,000 a day - go uneaten. When accounting for absences, the proportion of uneaten meals is 11.1%. Around half a million hot school meals are delivered to primary schools across the country daily, with the scheme extended nationwide in September 2025 to benefit 3,200 schools and more than 550,000 children.

stories.title: H&M founding family builds stake as turnaround struggles
stories.summary: The billionaire family behind H&M is quietly increasing its stake, fuelling speculation it could take the fast-fashion retailer private as CEO Daniel Erver's turnaround efforts have so far failed to boost the shares or lift sales significantly. The Persson family's Ramsbury Invest holding company, primarily owned by Sweden's richest person Stefan Persson, has bought 36.8 million H&M shares so far this year, regulatory filings show. Stefan Persson is the son of H&M founder Erling Persson and the father of chairman Karl-Johan Persson. The family and related entities owned more than 68% of H&M's shares at the end of August, according to the company's website, up from 49.5% at the start of 2021. "It is very difficult to view it any other way than that their strategy is to slowly buy out the company," said Sverre Linton, chief legal officer of the Swedish Shareholders' Association, which represents small shareholders. "You could call it Sweden's slowest buyout." Under Swedish rules, shareholders who own 90% of a company can compel the purchase of the remaining shares.

stories.title: UN chief seeks AI curbs, end to wars in assembly address
stories.summary: United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres used his final address to the General Assembly to urge world leaders to regulate artificial intelligence, end wars, focus on climate change and overhaul UN institutions he warned are struggling to confront mounting global challenges. The former Portuguese prime minister, whose second five-year term ends on 31 December, reiterated his calls for global oversight of AI risks, just as the UN's 15-member Security Council prepares to host AI leadersfor a briefing on the powerful technology. Mr Guterres also reflected on the gridlock within the organisation, as nearly 130 world leaders gathered in New York, and Chinese President Xi Jinping and others - including leaders from South Africa, India and Germany - skipped the diplomatic meeting. Delegates responded with sustained applause when Mr Guterres defended a two-state solution for Israelis and Palestinians, demanded that "polluters must pay" for climate change and pressed for reforms to international institutions, causes he has championed throughout his decade leading the United Nations. The address capped a decade-long tenure in which Mr Guterres sought to position the UN as a mediator in conflicts and a forum for governing emerging technologies, even as major powers increasingly bypassed the organisation and Washington slashed its funding. "Those countries leading this technological revolution must share information on emerging safety risks, cooperate on testing and evaluation - and work towards common safeguards that protect us all," Mr Guterres told the assembly.

stories.title: Leinster looking to 'prove a point' in opening URC rounds
stories.summary: Having made a slow start to last year's URC season, Leinster hooker Gus McCarthy has stressed that the defending champions will have a point to prove this time around. Leo Cullen's men open their title defence away to the Lions in Johannesburg before a trip back down to sea level to face the Sharks in Durban. Leinster started last season in South Africa too, but fell to consecutive defeats to the Stormers (35-0) and Bulls (39-31), which gives them plenty of motivation this time around. "The way we started the season last year away to the Stormers was very, very disappointing", McCarthy said. "It's something we’ve reflected on and we’re looking to put that to bed. "It’s a big two games for us now. Hopefully we can prove a point and improve our performances."

stories.title: Loughgiel and St John's to learn punishments
stories.summary: Antrim clubs Loughgiel and St John's will be made aware on Tuesday of the sanctions arising from the on-field fracas in their hurling championship clash - with another investigation still working on punishments for the violence that erupted in the crowd after the full-time whistle. Loughgiel won the group game 0-30 to 3-14 but afterwards, players and mentors clashed in the middle of the pitch. At tonight’s county committee meeting, both clubs were informed that initial proposed sanctions were imminent for the on-field scenes, something pertinent to holders Johnnies given they are in quarter-final action this Saturday against Glenariffe giving them a small window to appeal. Loughgiel have qualified straight to the semi-finals with details to be confirmed of when that will be played, and who against. Meanwhile, the Ulster county are also set to announce their new Under-20 hurling manager on Tuesday.

stories.title: Nienaber: 'We're working as hard as we can'
stories.summary: Leinster coach Jacques Nienaber has said that despite being two-time defending champions, his squad are working as hard as they can to retain their crown. Speaking on Monday ahead of their season opener against the Lions, the former South African coach admitted he is happy with where Leinster are at currently. "We know it's an extremely tough competition to be a part of, but this pre-season we're building slowly but surely, but it's been good and the guys are working really, really hard. "We're just excited that the pre-season has now come to an end and it's game week now." The aim for every team, according to Nienaber, is to be "in a better spot than what they were in last year", but that will be tricky for a side who won the title on home soil for a second year running. However, Leinster's title defence was not without flaws, losing six of the 18 regular season games, including both of their contests down in South Africa.

stories.title: U2 at 50: The 10 best U2 songs of all time, ranked
stories.summary: Freelance journalist and broadcaster, writing about music and the arts. Happy Birthday, U2! One of the biggest rock bands of all time celebrates 50 years in business this month, with 15 studio albums, 12 EPs, three compilations, two live albums and no less than 85 singles released by the Dublin band over the course of that half-century. The question is, which songs are their best? It may be overplayed, it may be somewhat overcooked, it may not have the emotional heft of some of their other tracks - but only a curmudgeon would argue against Beautiful Day being one of U2’s most euphoric songs. Taken from 2001’s pivotal All That You Can’t Leave Behind album, it ushered in a new era for the band while cementing their position as one of the finest stadium rock bands on the planet. That intro alone is worth its weight in gold: the yearning squeal of The Edge’s guitar, the piano riff, the tremulous bassline, that primitive yowl of Bono’s…. 43 years after it was first released, New Year’s Day sounds as fresh as ever. The first track from U2’s third album War also incorporated social and political themes, written about the revolutionary Polish solidarity movement in 1980 which eventually led to the collapse of communism in Poland. Apparently it was originally intended as a love song about Ali Hewson. No harm, no foul, Ali. U2 have always looked to the wider world for inspiration, but this song - also taken from War - brought them closer to home and is perhaps their most explicitly political song to date. Written about the Troubles and specifically the Bloody Sunday atrocity of 1972, it’s a protest song about the futility of war, wrapped up in a spiky rock tune. From Larry Mullen’s martial cadence to Bono’s exasperated lyrics ("How long, how long must we sing this song?"), it still packs a mighty punch. By 1987, U2 had spent much of the decade touring extensively in America and absorbing its culture from the inside looking out. The result was The Joshua Tree - the album that many fans still consider their defining moment. The swarthy shuck of the guitar riff on this song, coupled with the gospel undertones and Bono’s preacher-like lyrics as it slips into the deep groove of Adam Clayton’s bassline is simply sensational stuff.

stories.title: Say Cheese: Ireland's destination cheese counters
stories.summary: Patrick Hanlon and Russell Alford are freelance food and travel writers who write at gastrogays.com and can be found on social media as @gastrogays As many of us can attest, cheese is life. Ireland is alive with passionate purveyors of cheese operating destination deli counters and delighting customers with the most delicious finds and flavours. From Donegal to Dingle, Bushmills to Kells, here are our top picks of epic cheese counters. Johnny McDowell MBE and business partner Laura Bradley operate a pair of delis dedicated to Irish produce, where everything on the shelves and in the massive cheese counter comes from the island of Ireland. Having grown from an online shop based out of Johnny’s parents’ attic when e-commerce for gourmet food products was a fairly novel idea, the pair opened the original in the bustling market town of Comber in 2014. They moved to their current, larger premises in the town in 2018 and opened a second site, on Belfast’s Ormeau Road, in 2020. Theirs is one of the most extensive and keenest curations of produce in all of Ireland. If Johnny and Laura endorse a producer enough to sell their wares and slice their cheese, you know it’s fantastic.

stories.title: AI, US war against Iran to dominate UN General Assembly
stories.summary: The future of artificial intelligence and the stalled US war against Iran, with its ripple effect on the global economy, are expected to dominate the UN gathering of world leaders. Following weeks of worldwide headlines about risks of uncontrollable AI - and calls for a slowdown - industry leaders are set to brief an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council. Sam Altman of OpenAI, Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face will brief the 15-strong council, the United Nation's top body. Hugging Face, a repository of AI models, was the target of a recent cyberattack by autonomous OpenAI software, the first in a series of incidents that have raised alarm bells over the rapidly evolving technology. Meanwhile, the annual parade of UN General Assembly speeches is set to continue, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arriving last night, according to Iranian state media, to address the world body for the first time since the United States and Israel launched a war on his country. The attacks in late February sparked a war that engulfed the Middle East, and the Trump administration has so far yet to reach a deal with Iran to end the conflict.

stories.summary: A man who escaped from garda custody at Newcastle West District Court was detained at his home after being on the run for around six hours. He fled the courthouse after being brought before the court to face an assault charge. The court had heard evidence of his arrest, charge and caution before it was discovered that he was not present in the courtroom. It is understood he had requested to use the toilet and had fled through a bathroom window. A garda helicopter was deployed over west Limerick as part of the search operation. The man, who is believed to be in his 30s and from Limerick city, was re-arrested around 6pm yesterday evening.

stories.title: Calls for Govt to reject proposed minimum wage increase
stories.summary: The Small Firms Association has called on the Government to reject the proposed increase in the national minimum wage in the forthcoming budget to help small businesses cope with rising labour-related costs. In its pre-budget submission, the SFA said there is a critical need to halt further wage hikes proposed by the Low Pay Commission to ensure the survival of viable enterprises. In July, it was reported that the Low Pay Commission had recommended that the minimum wage should increase by 5.6%. If the proposals are accepted by the Government, it would see the rate rise by 79 cent an hour from €14.15 to €14.94. In its submission, the SFA said that the minimum wage has moved from €9.15 in 2016 to €14.15 in 2026. "While the national minimum wage increased by 54.6% in the same period, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased by roughly 25% cumulatively from 2016 to 2026," according to the SFA.

stories.title: JD Sports first half profit hit by American weakness
stories.summary: British sports and fashion retailer JD Sports reported a 19.7% drop in first-half profit today, hurt by weakness in its key North American market, but maintained the full-year earnings outlook it downgraded last month. The group's shares are down 10% over the last year, reflecting pressure on its core younger and less affluent customer base, a market driven by promotions, and a lack of innovation from Nike, which is overhauling its business and accounts for more than 40% of JD's sales. JD made a profit before tax and adjusting items of £282m in the six months to August 1 on sales down 0.7% to £5.9 billion. Group like-for-like sales fell 3.1% in its second quarter, with North America down 6.8%. JD makes over a third of its sales in North America where it trades as JD Sports, Hibbett, DTLR, Shoe Palace and Finish Line. CEO Regis Schultz said JD's first-half performance was resilient against "a challenging backdrop of consumer cost-of-living pressures, footwear product-cycle headwinds and a highly promotional market."

stories.title: US 'golden dome' system permitted in Greenland under deal
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump and the leaders of Greenland and Denmark have signed an agreement ⁠that permits a larger US military presence on Greenland and may resolve a standoff over the strategically located and mineral-rich island. The agreement, signed during Mr Trump's visit to the UN General Assembly in New York, stops short of Mr Trump's demand that the US adopt Greenland as a US territory to head off the growing Arctic presence of Russia and China. But the deal does permit a greater US military presence on the icy territory, an option that emerged as Greenland leaders argued against a complete US takeover. A text of the deal released after the signing event said the US can establish a "Golden Dome" defense system in Greenland as a shield against ballistic missile threats. The shortest route from Europe to North America runs via the Arctic island, which is the location of the northernmost US military base. In his speech to the assembled world leaders at the UN before the signing ceremony, Mr Trump said the agreement gives the US "permanent control over security and all other needs on that territory."

stories.title: Celtic chief offers support to embattled manager O'Neill
stories.summary: Chief executive Michael Nicholson has given an indication that Martin O'Neill is set to remain in charge of Celtic after vowing to "support" the embattled manager. The 74-year-old cast doubt on his own future when he spoke about entering a period of self-reflection after the Hoops’ meek 1-0 defeat at home to Rangers in the William Hill Premiership on Sunday. Following a third consecutive loss in eight days, and just a few weeks after the Champions League play-off collapse against LASK, a beleaguered O’Neill said "I genuinely will reflect and see" before joking "I’ll be 110 in two years’ time so it might be time to wrap it up." With pressure also building from a frustrated fanbase, there was an expectation in many quarters that the veteran manager, who recently spent time in hospital for a minor health procedure, may decide that the current three-week international break represents an obvious window for him to step aside. But as Celtic released their annual accounts on Tuesday night showing a loss of £4.8m (€5.6m) for the year ending 30 June, 2026, the accompanying chief executive’s review from Nicholson suggested that O’Neill is set to stay put. "Having started well in the Premiership this season, we experienced disappointment in the UEFA Champions League play-off," it read. "Reaching the league phase of the Champions League is an objective for us all, and we are sorry not to have achieved it.
